1.open: Tell about a time you were told to wait for something. Were you good at it?
questions: Jesus showed himself alive "with many convincing proofs" over forty days (v. 3). Why might the first followers have needed that much time and evidence? What helps you trust that something is true?
Jesus told them, "Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised" (v. 4). What makes waiting hard? When has waiting turned out to matter more than you expected?
The disciples asked, "Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (v. 6). What were they hoping for, and why might that question have been natural for them?

Jesus answered, "It is not for you to know times or seasons" (v. 7), then pointed them to a task. Christians differ on whether his answer leaves room for a future earthly kingdom for Israel or redirects that hope into a worldwide mission. Whichever way you lean, what do you notice about how he moves them from questions about the future to what to do now?

Jesus says, "you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses" (v. 8). Notice that the power comes first and the witnessing follows. What does it mean to you to be a witness, and what feels hard or doable about it?
The two men ask, "why do you stand here looking into the sky?" (v. 11). Where are we tempted to stare at heaven, or at the future, instead of getting on with the life in front of us?

Verse 14 says they "all continued in prayer," and the group included women, Mary, and Jesus' brothers. What stands out to you about who was in that room, and what does it say about who belongs among Jesus' followers?

When the group chose a replacement for Judas, they prayed, "Lord, You know everyone's heart" (v. 24). How do you make decisions when you are not sure what is right? If you are honest, how much does prayer feel like part of that for you right now?
1.life: Jesus' friends waited and prayed together before they did anything else. This week, set aside a regular time to pray with one other person, even for ten minutes, and ask God what your next small step as a witness might be.
1.prayer: Thank God for Jesus, who is alive, and for the gift of his Spirit. Ask for patience in the places you are waiting, and for courage to be a witness where you live and work.
1.tip: Verses 18 and 19 are graphic, and people may ask how they fit with Matthew's account of Judas. Say plainly that readers have long differed on this, give it a minute, then bring the group back to the main thread of Jesus' promise and the disciples' waiting.

2.open: Think of a time you heard something in your own language or accent, far from home, and it felt like a welcome. What was that like?
questions: The crowd hears the believers "declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues" (v. 11). Why might it matter that people heard the good news in the language of their own hearts and homes?

Some in the crowd were "astounded and perplexed" and asked, "What does this mean?" (v. 12), while others mocked and said they were drunk (v. 13). What do you think shapes which way a person goes when something unexpected happens?

Peter quotes Joel: God will "pour out My Spirit on all people," including sons and daughters, young and old, and even servants (vv. 17, 18). Who might have been surprised to be included? Who do we tend to leave out?

Peter says Jesus was "delivered up by God's set plan" and put to death by human hands, and that "God raised Him from the dead" (vv. 23, 24). How do you understand a story where both God's plan and human choices are at work? Many Christians say this passage must never be used to blame Jewish people, then or now. How would you explain why?

When the people heard Peter, "they were cut to the heart" and asked, "what shall we do?" (v. 37). Have you ever felt that kind of stirring, or do you feel unsure about all of this right now? Be as honest as you like.

Peter says, "Repent and be baptized" and then "you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (v. 38). Christians understand baptism and forgiveness in different ways. What does the word repent mean to you, and how does it sound as an invitation rather than a scolding?
The believers "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer" (v. 42). Which of these four comes easiest to you, and which is hardest?

Verses 44 and 45 say the believers "had everything in common" and shared with "anyone who was in need." Christians differ on whether this is a pattern for every church or a snapshot of one moment. Either way, what is one realistic way our group could share what we have?
2.life: Look for one person this week who may be on the edge of things, such as a newcomer, someone lonely or someone in need. Share a meal, a ride or some practical help with them, and notice what it costs and what it gives.
2.prayer: Thank God for pouring out his Spirit on ordinary people of every age and background. Ask him to make your group a place where people are welcomed, fed and cared for, and to stir in each of you a trust in Jesus that is honest and real.
2.tip: Questions about speaking in tongues and baptism can take over the evening. Name plainly that Christians in the room may hold different views, ask people to say what they have seen or experienced rather than to argue, and bring the group back to Peter's message and the community that formed. Also be ready to gently shut down any use of verse 23 to blame Jewish people.

3.open: Who is someone who has stopped to notice you or help you when most people kept walking?
questions: The man had been "lame from birth" and was put at the gate "every day to beg" (v. 2). What do you think his days were like, and how do you picture the people who walked past him?
Peter "looked directly at him" and said, "Look at us!" (v. 4). Why might it matter that he stopped and really saw the man? Who is easy to overlook where you live or work?
Peter says, "Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you" (v. 6). What do you have to give, even if it is not money?
The man was "walking and leaping and praising God" (v. 8), and people "were filled with wonder and amazement" (v. 10). What do you think it felt like to be him, and to watch him?

Peter asks, "Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?" (v. 12). Why is it so easy to give credit to people instead of God, and what changes when we do not?

Peter tells the crowd, "I know that you acted in ignorance" (v. 17), and then invites them to "Repent, then, and turn back" (v. 19). What do you notice about how he speaks to people who share in a terrible wrong? What does that say about God's kindness?
Verse 16 speaks of "the faith that comes through Him." Faith can feel weak or uncertain. Where are you honestly at with faith right now, and what would help?
Verses 19 to 21 speak of "times of refreshing" and "the restoration of all things." What does that hope mean to you when things in your life or in the world feel broken?
3.life: This week, choose one person you normally pass by without a second look. Stop, look at them, learn their name, and offer them something real, whether time, a meal or a kind word.
3.prayer: Thank God for lifting up people who are stuck and overlooked, and for lifting us. Ask for eyes to see people and the humility to give Jesus the credit.
3.tip: Verses 13 to 15 can be heard as blaming Jews as a people for Jesus' death, and that reading has caused real harm. Remind the group that Peter is himself Jewish, speaking to a particular Jerusalem crowd, and that he offers them forgiveness and welcome right away. Also, Christians differ on what the "times of refreshing" in verses 19 to 21 point to, so say so briefly and keep the focus on the call to turn to God.

4.open: Tell us about a time you were nervous to speak up, whether at work, school, or with family. What happened?
questions: The leaders were "greatly disturbed" that Peter and John were proclaiming the resurrection (v. 2). Why might this message have felt so threatening to them, and why might it still stir up strong reactions today?

The council saw their boldness and "realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men" and noted "that these men had been with Jesus" (v. 13). What does it look like for an ordinary person to show they have been with Jesus?

Peter says, "Salvation exists in no one else" (v. 12). Christians read this differently: some say it means only those who consciously trust Jesus are saved, and others say any salvation comes through Jesus, even for some who never knew of him. How does this verse land with you, whichever way you lean?
The leaders "had nothing to say in response" because the healed man stood right there (v. 14). Why can a changed life say more than a good argument?

Peter and John answer, "we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard" (v. 20). What have you seen or heard of God, even something small, that you find hard to keep to yourself? If nothing comes to mind right now, what makes that hard to say?

When the believers heard the threats, they prayed, "enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness" (v. 29). They asked for courage, not for safety. What do you usually ask God for when you feel afraid?
Verse 32 says the believers were united in heart and soul, and that they shared what they owned. What might sharing look like in our group or church today, with time, money, meals or rides?
Barnabas is called "Son of Encouragement" (v. 36). Who has played that role in your life, and who might need it from you?
4.life: Pick one person this week to encourage the way Barnabas did, with a note, a call, a meal, or practical help. Also ask God for one small moment of courage to say something true about your faith.
4.prayer: Thank God for ordinary people who have been with Jesus. Ask for the kind of courage the believers prayed for, and for open hands toward those in need.
4.tip: Verse 12 may bring strong feelings, especially from anyone with loved ones who do not believe. Name plainly that Christians read it differently, make room for honest sadness or doubt, and steer the group back to Peter's main point: the healing and the hope come through Jesus.

5.open: Have you ever pretended to know more, or to be doing better, than you really were? What happened?
questions: Peter says the land and the money were always theirs to keep: "Did it not belong to you before it was sold?" (v. 4). If the money was theirs, what was the actual wrong in what Ananias and Sapphira did?
What makes people want to look more generous or committed than they really are? Where do you feel that pull, at church, at work or online?
"Great fear came over all who heard what had happened" (v. 5). Many readers find this story hard and unsettling. What do you feel when you read it, and what questions does it leave you with?

Christians differ on how to read the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira. Some see a unique judgment at the church's beginning, others ask what it says about God and dishonesty today. How do you make sense of it, or is it simply something you cannot yet make sense of?
In verse 15, people hoped "at least Peter's shadow might fall on some of them." What does this show about how desperate people were, and where do you go when you are desperate for help?
The apostles were jailed, then freed, then went straight back to teaching (vv. 18-21). What do you think gave them such steadiness when the authorities opposed them?
Peter says, "We must obey God rather than men" (v. 29). What does that look like in everyday life today, and how do we tell the difference between obeying God and just digging in our heels?

After being flogged, the apostles left "rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name" (v. 41). How can anyone rejoice in that? Have you ever seen someone stay hopeful through unfair treatment?
5.life: This week, pay attention to one moment when you are tempted to look better than you are, whether in what you say, post or give. Try telling the plain truth instead, and notice how it feels.
5.prayer: Thank God that he sees us exactly as we are and still welcomes us. Ask for honesty in the small things and courage to follow him when it costs something.
5.tip: The deaths in verses 5 to 10 will likely dominate the conversation, and some may be troubled or angry. Don't rush to defend or explain it. Say plainly that Christians read it differently, let people voice their unease, then steer back to the point Peter makes about pretending before God and the community.

6.open: Think of a time you were left out of something small, like a group photo, a message thread or a meal. How did it feel?
questions: The chapter opens with people who "began to grumble" because their widows "were being overlooked" (v. 1). Why do you think the complaint was raised out loud instead of being swallowed? What does that say about the early church?
The Twelve said, "It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables" (v. 2). What do you think they meant, and what do you notice about how they handled the problem?

The apostles asked for men "full of the Spirit and wisdom" to handle food (v. 3). Why might a practical job like this need people of that kind? What does it suggest about everyday work being part of serving God?

All seven names are Greek, which may mean the group chose leaders from the community that had complained. How does it feel to be trusted with fixing a problem you pointed out? When have you seen that go well, or not?
Verse 7 says "the word of God continued to spread" after the dispute was settled. Why might fixing an unfair situation help the message move forward?

Stephen's opponents "could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke" (v. 10), so they turned to false witnesses. Why do people sometimes attack a person when they cannot answer the argument? Have you seen this happen?

In verse 15 the council saw that Stephen's face "was like the face of an angel," even while he stood accused. Readers take this in different ways. What do you make of it? Where have you seen peace in someone under pressure?
If you are quiet, unsure or not sure where you fit, answer honestly: in a group like ours, who might be easy to overlook, and what would help them feel noticed?
6.life: This week, look for one person who tends to be overlooked, at church, work, school or in your neighborhood. Do one small, concrete thing so they know they are seen, such as a call, a meal or a seat saved beside you.
6.prayer: Ask God to open your eyes to people who are being missed. Pray for wisdom and a steady heart for anyone in the group who is facing opposition or unfair treatment.
6.tip: Christians differ on whether the seven were the first deacons or were simply chosen for one practical need, and this can pull the group into a debate about church structure. Mention it in one line, then bring the group back to the heart of the chapter: noticing the overlooked and serving them well.

7.open: Who is someone you have known who stayed calm and kind when others were being unfair to them?
questions: Stephen begins with Abraham, who was called while still in Mesopotamia, far from the promised land (v. 2). Why might Stephen start his answer here, when he was asked whether the charges were true?
Of Joseph, Stephen says his brothers sold him into Egypt, "But God was with him" (vv. 9, 10). Where have you seen God present in a place or season that looked like the wrong one?

Moses thought his people would understand that God was using him, "but they did not" (v. 25). Then they asked, "Who made you ruler and judge?" (v. 27). Why do you think people sometimes turn away from the very help God sends?
At the burning bush God says, "the place where you are standing is holy ground" (v. 33). That was in a desert, far from any temple. What does it tell us about where God can meet people?

In verse 48 Stephen says, "the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands." Which things, such as buildings, routines or traditions, can we lean on so much that we forget God himself? Christians also differ on whether Stephen is rejecting the temple or only the idea that a building can contain God. How do you read it?

Stephen tells the council, "You always resist the Holy Spirit" (v. 51). It is a hard thing to say. How can we hear a hard word like that without getting defensive, and when have you resisted something you later saw was from God?

Stephen sees Jesus "standing at the right hand of God" (v. 55) and prays, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them" (v. 60). What do you make of someone responding to violence this way? Be honest if it seems strange, too much, or out of reach.
The witnesses lay their garments at the feet of "a young man named Saul" (v. 58). What does it do to you to know the story does not end with this scene?
7.life: Think of one person who has hurt or wronged you. This week, pray for them by name once a day. You do not need to feel forgiving. Simply ask God to do good in their life, and notice what shifts in you.
7.prayer: Thank God that he is with us in every place, not only in church buildings. Ask for a heart that stays open to the Holy Spirit, and for the grace to pray for those who hurt us.
7.tip: Verses 51 to 53 can sound harsh, and some people may hear them as a judgment on Jewish people today. Remind the group that Stephen was himself a Jew speaking to fellow Jews, using the same words Moses and the prophets used about their own people. Keep the focus on our own tendency to resist God, and on Stephen's forgiveness. Also, do not get stuck on the small differences from Genesis in verses 1 to 16. Say they exist, scholars discuss them, and move on.

8.open: Have you ever ended up somewhere you never planned to be, and been glad you did?
questions: After Stephen's death, "a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem" (v. 1). Then "those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went" (v. 4). What stands out to you about how these believers responded to being driven from home?

Philip "proclaimed the Christ" in a Samaritan city, and "there was great joy in that city" (vv. 5, 8). Jews and Samaritans had been rivals for centuries. Who are the people we might find it hard to welcome, or to be welcomed by?

Simon was baptized and "followed Philip closely," yet he was "astounded by the great signs and miracles he observed" (v. 13). What is the difference between being amazed by God's power and trusting God himself?

Simon said, "Give me this power as well" (v. 19), and Peter answered that he "thought you could buy the gift of God with money" (v. 20). In what quiet ways do we still try to earn or pay for what God gives freely?

Peter told Simon, "Repent, therefore, of your wickedness, and pray to the Lord. Perhaps He will forgive you" (v. 22). Simon answered, "Pray to the Lord for me" (v. 24). How do you read Simon's reply? Is it sorrow, fear, or something else?

Philip asked the Ethiopian, "Do you understand what you are reading?" He replied that he could not "unless someone guides me" (vv. 30, 31). Where has someone helped you understand something in the Bible? What parts still confuse you, and is it okay to say so here?

The Ethiopian said, "Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?" (v. 36). He was an outsider in many ways. What do you think made him bold enough to ask, and what might make us hold back?
He "went on his way rejoicing" (v. 39). Where do you see joy in this chapter, and where do you find it hard to feel joy in your own faith right now?
8.life: Think of one person outside your usual circle, maybe a coworker, neighbor or classmate. This week, take one small step toward them, like a real conversation, an invitation, or listening to their questions about faith.
8.prayer: Thank God that his gift cannot be bought and is offered freely to everyone. Ask him to show you where he is using a hard season to move you somewhere new, and to give you the humility to learn from others.
8.tip: Simon's story and the Spirit coming after baptism can pull the group into a long debate. Say plainly that Christians disagree about what the delay in Samaria means, some seeing a normal second experience and others a one-time sign that Samaritans were included. Then bring the group back to the chapter's main thread: God's gift is free, and the message keeps reaching new people.

9.open: Have you ever had to start over somewhere new, like a new school, job or town? What was the hardest part?
questions: Saul was "still breathing out murderous threats" when Jesus stopped him (v. 1). What does it say about God that he met Saul in the middle of his worst chapter and not after he cleaned up?
Jesus asks, "why do you persecute Me?" (v. 4). What do you make of Jesus speaking as though harm done to his followers was done to him?
Saul is blind and goes without food or drink for three days (v. 9). Have you ever had a stretch of waiting or confusion where you could not see the way forward? What was that like?

Ananias answers the Lord with an honest objection, listing the harm Saul had done (vv. 13-14). What do you notice about the Lord letting him say it? How could that help someone who is unsure or has doubts about what God is asking?
Ananias still goes and begins with the words "Brother Saul" (v. 17). Who is a person that would be hard for you to call brother or sister, and what might it cost you to do it?

The believers in Jerusalem were "all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple" (v. 26), until Barnabas spoke up for him. Why was their fear understandable, and who has been a Barnabas for you, or could be for someone else?
The Lord says Saul is "My chosen instrument" and that he "must suffer for My name" (vv. 15-16). How do you hear that mix of calling and hardship? How does it sit with you?

Tabitha is remembered as "always occupied with works of kindness and charity" (v. 36), and the widows show Peter what she made (v. 39). What small, ordinary kindness has shaped your life, and why might God count it as important?
9.life: Think of one person you have written off, or one person others have written off. This week, take one small step toward them, such as a prayer, a message or a kind word. If you know someone who is trying to start fresh, be a Barnabas and speak up for them.
9.prayer: Thank God that he comes to people who are not looking for him. Ask for honest eyes to see where you are stuck or blind, and for the willingness to welcome someone you find hard to trust.
9.tip: The group may get stuck on whether Saul's change was a conversion from one religion to another or a calling within his Jewish faith to take its message to the nations. Say plainly that Christians read it differently, then bring the group back to what all can see: Jesus stopped Saul, Ananias obeyed, and Barnabas took a risk on him. Also go gently with the question about someone who is hard to welcome, since a person in the room may have been hurt by someone like Saul.

10.open: Think of a time you were the new person in a room, at a school, a job or a church. What helped you feel welcome, or what made it harder?
questions: Cornelius was not Jewish, yet he "prayed to God regularly" and gave generously (v. 2). What do you notice about a man who was seeking God before he knew much about Jesus?
The angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and gifts "have ascended as a memorial offering before God" (v. 4). What does it say about God that he notices someone outside the usual circle?
Peter answers the voice with "No, Lord!" (v. 14). Why might a good and sincere believer say no to God, and when have you felt pulled between what you were taught and what God seemed to be asking?
The voice says, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean" (v. 15). In verse 28 Peter applies this to people. Who do people today tend to treat as unclean or off limits, even in church?

Peter went with the men "without hesitation" (v. 20) and stepped into a Gentile home, which he would normally have avoided (v. 28). What is one small step toward someone different from you that would take courage?
Peter stops Cornelius from bowing and says, "I am only a man myself" (v. 26). Why does it matter that Peter refuses to be treated as more than he is?
Peter says, "God does not show favoritism" (v. 34). Where do you find that easy to believe, and where is it harder, whether for others or for yourself?
The Spirit falls on the listeners before they are baptized or even finish hearing the message (v. 44). If you are honest, what questions or doubts does that stir up for you about how God works?
10.life: This week, think of one person or group you tend to keep at a distance. Pray for them by name each day, then take one small step, such as a greeting, a conversation or an invitation to share a meal.
10.prayer: Thank God that he welcomes people from every nation and notices those who seek him. Ask him to show you where you have drawn lines he has not drawn, and to give you the willingness to cross them.
10.tip: Verse 35 is easy to turn into a fight about whether people who have never heard of Jesus are saved. Say in one line that Christians read it differently, then bring the group back to what the chapter clearly shows: God opens the door, Peter walks through it, and the whole household is welcomed.

11.open: Who is someone who made you feel welcome the first time you walked into a new place, and what did they do?
questions: The believers in Judea objected, "You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them" (v. 3). Why would sharing a meal matter so much to them? What does a shared table say about people today?
Peter did not argue from theory. He "explained to them the whole sequence of events" (v. 4). What do you notice about how he handled criticism?
In his vision Peter heard, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean" (v. 9). What kinds of people or groups do we tend to treat as outside the circle, even without saying so?
Peter asks, "who was I to hinder the work of God?" (v. 17). Have you ever caught yourself standing in the way of something God seemed to be doing? What was that like?
When the critics heard Peter, "they had no further objections, and they glorified God" (v. 18). Changing your mind is hard. What do you think made it possible for them?
Barnabas "saw the grace of God" in Antioch and "rejoiced" (v. 23). He could have come to inspect and criticize. What does his response show, and who has been a Barnabas for you?
Verse 26 says the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. If someone watched your life this week, what might they call you, and does it match what you hope?
The church in Antioch sent relief to believers in Judea, "each according to his ability" (v. 29). Where is it hard for you to trust, believe or give, and what would help you take one honest step?
11.life: Think of one person or group you tend to keep at a distance. This week, share a meal or a real conversation with someone from that circle, and simply listen.
11.prayer: Thank God for welcoming us when we were outsiders. Ask for open eyes to see what God is doing in people we might overlook, and for a Barnabas heart toward them.
11.tip: Christians differ on whether Peter's vision ended the Jewish food laws for everyone or mainly taught that non-Jewish people must not be treated as unclean. Name that in one line and move on. The chapter's main point is welcome, so steer the group back to the table and to Barnabas.

12.open: Can you remember a time you were so excited about good news that you forgot what you were supposed to be doing?
questions: Herod had James "put to death with the sword" (v. 2) and then went after Peter. What do you notice about how quickly the chapter moves from one event to the next, and how might the church have felt?
Verse 5 says Peter "was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him." What does it look like to pray when there is little else you can do?
Peter was "sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains" on the night before his trial (v. 6). What do you make of him sleeping at a time like that?
Peter "was unaware that what the angel was doing was real" and thought he was seeing a vision (v. 9). When has something good happened that you found hard to believe at first?

The people praying told Rhoda, "You are out of your mind" (v. 15), and were "astounded" when they saw Peter (v. 16). What does it say about this group that they were praying and still surprised? What does that say to us about our own prayers?

James was killed and Peter walked free from the same prison system. How do you make sense of stories where one person is spared and another is not? Be as honest as you like, including if you have no answer.
Herod was struck down because he "did not give glory to God" (v. 23). Where are we tempted to take praise that belongs to God, or to rely on power that does not last?
Verse 24 says "the word of God continued to spread and multiply." Why might the writer end the chapter this way, right after a king dies? What encouragement do you take from it?
12.life: Pick one person or situation that feels stuck or out of your hands. Pray for it each day this week, and tell one friend so they can pray too. At the end of the week, notice how it felt to keep praying without knowing the outcome.
12.prayer: Thank God that he hears the prayers of his people, even weak and doubtful ones. Ask for trust to keep praying, and name anyone who is suffering or in danger right now.
12.tip: Question 6 may bring up real grief, since some in the group may have prayed and not seen rescue. Don't rush to explain it away. Let people say they are confused or hurting, and remind the group that the chapter itself honors James and does not explain why he died.

13.open: Think of a time someone trusted you with a job you weren't sure you were ready for. How did it go?
questions: The church at Antioch included people from very different backgrounds, such as Lucius of Cyrene and Manaen, who was raised with Herod (v. 1). What do you notice about who God gathers and uses?

The Holy Spirit spoke while the church was worshiping and fasting, and told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work he had called them to (v. 2). What does it tell you that the call came while the church was worshiping and not while it was planning?
After fasting and prayer, the church laid hands on the two men and "sent them off" (v. 3). Who has sent you out or backed you in something? Who could you send or back right now?

On Cyprus, the proconsul was "a man of intelligence" who "wanted to hear the word of God" (v. 7), while Elymas tried to turn him from the faith (v. 8). Why do you think the same message draws some people in and pushes others away?
Paul's speech starts with Israel's story, from Egypt to David, before it gets to Jesus (vv. 17 to 23). Why might he begin there, and how would you tell your own story of how God has been at work?
Paul says, "through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you" (v. 38). What does forgiveness mean to you, and is it easy or hard to believe it is meant for you?

Some of the crowd were "filled with jealousy" when they saw the crowds (v. 45), while others "rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord" (v. 48). Where have you seen good news stir up both joy and resistance? If you are honestly unsure where you stand with this message, what holds you back?
Even after being driven out, "the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit" (v. 52). What do you think kept them joyful when things went badly?
13.life: Think of one person you could encourage or send off with a prayer this week, perhaps someone starting something new or facing something hard. Tell them you are backing them, and pray for them by name.
13.prayer: Thank God for the people who have sent you out and stood behind you. Ask the Spirit for open ears to hear his leading, and for joy that does not depend on how things go.
13.tip: Verses 9 to 11 and verse 48 can lead to heavy side debates, such as why Elymas was struck blind or what it means to be "appointed for eternal life," which Christians understand in different ways. Name that briefly, then steer back to the main thread: God sends people out, and the message of forgiveness lands differently on different hearts.

14.open: Have you ever been given more credit than you deserved, or been completely misunderstood? What happened?
questions: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas "spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed," yet others "poisoned their minds against the brothers" (vv. 1-2). Why do you think the same message can draw some people in and push others away?
When the plot to stone them came out, they "fled" and "continued to preach the gospel" (vv. 5-7). What does it tell you that they left one place without giving up the work?
Paul "saw that he had faith to be healed" (v. 9). The man had never walked, and he listened anyway. What do you make of a faith that is simply listening and hoping?
The crowd shouted, "The gods have come down to us in human form!" (v. 11). Why do you think people are so quick to turn gifted or helpful people into heroes? Where do you see that today?
Paul and Barnabas said, "We too are only men, human like you" (v. 15). When someone praises you, what do you usually do with it? What would it look like to point it back to God?

Paul told the crowd that God "has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness," giving "rain from heaven and fruitful seasons" (v. 17). What everyday good things make you feel that someone is looking after you? If nothing does right now, how would you say that honestly?
The disciples "gathered around him" after the stoning, and Paul got up (v. 20). Who has gathered around you when things went badly, and who could you gather around this week?
They told new believers, "We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God" (v. 22). How does that land with you: as honest, discouraging, or something else? Why?
14.life: Think of one person who is struggling in their faith or going through a hard stretch. This week, reach out with a call, a visit or a meal, and simply stay near them, the way the disciples did for Paul.
14.prayer: Thank God for his kindness shown in ordinary things like rain, food and gladness. Ask for humility when others praise us, and for steadiness and good company when following him gets hard.
14.tip: Verse 22 can sound like a warning that discourages newer or struggling members. Say plainly that Paul and Barnabas were encouraging people, not scaring them, and that the chapter ends with a church gathered and glad. Let anyone say honestly that hardship has shaken their faith, and do not rush to fix it.

15.open: Think of a time you joined a new group, team or workplace. What unwritten rule did you only learn by getting it wrong?
questions: Some men taught, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved" (v. 1). Why might someone who loved God sincerely believe this?

Peter says God "made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith" (v. 9). What did the Gentiles' experience of the Spirit show the leaders, and why did it carry so much weight?
Peter calls the law "a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear" (v. 10). What are some yokes people carry today, in church or outside it, that God never asked them to carry?

Verse 11 says, "we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are." In your own words, what does it mean that everyone is saved the same way? Is that easy or hard to believe about yourself?

Notice how the decision is made. People argue, listen to stories, look at Scripture, and then agree on a way forward (vv. 7, 12, 15). What can that teach us about handling disagreements in a church or group?

James asks the Gentile believers to avoid four things so that Jewish and non Jewish believers could share life together (vv. 19, 20). Christians disagree on whether these were a temporary arrangement or lasting rules. What do you see in the text that helps you think about it?

The leaders write that it "seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you" (v. 28). When have you seen a church add a burden that Scripture did not? When have you seen one welcome people well?

Paul and Barnabas have a disagreement "so sharp that they parted company" (v. 39). What do you make of the fact that the Bible reports this without tidying it up? Has a disagreement with someone you respect ever changed a friendship?
15.life: Think of one person who might feel like an outsider where you gather, at church, work or in your neighborhood. This week, reach out to them with an invitation, a meal or a simple conversation, and ask nothing of them first.
15.prayer: Thank God that we are saved "through the grace of the Lord Jesus" and not by anything we achieve. Ask for a welcoming heart toward newcomers, and for humility and kindness when you disagree with someone you love.
15.tip: Verses 20 and 29 raise questions about what to do with the four requests, and some people may also get stuck on the sharp split in verses 36 to 41. Say plainly that Christians differ on the four requests, then bring the group back to the main point: the leaders decided that salvation comes by grace and that newcomers should not be burdened. For the Paul and Barnabas quarrel, resist ruling on who was right, since the text does not say.

16.open: Tell about a time you took a wrong turn, or a plan changed at the last minute, and it turned out better or stranger than you expected.
questions: Twice the Spirit stopped Paul from going where he planned (vv. 6-7). Then he saw a man pleading, "Come over to Macedonia and help us" (v. 9). Think of a time a door closed on you. What did you do, and what did you learn?

Lydia was already a "worshiper of God," and then "the Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message" (v. 14). What do you think it means for God to open a heart? Who or what opened yours, or is still working on it?
After her baptism Lydia said, "come and stay at my house" (v. 15). What does her response tell you about how faith and everyday life fit together? What could hospitality look like for you right now?

The slave girl's owners were angry because "their hope of making money was gone" (v. 19). Paul helped her, and it cost him a beating. Where do you see people today being used for someone else's profit? What might it cost to stand with them?

Paul and Silas had been beaten and locked in the inner cell, yet at midnight they were "praying and singing hymns to God" while others listened (v. 25). What do you think that looked like in real life? When have you seen someone stay steady in a hard place?

The jailer asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" (v. 30). They answered, "Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household" (v. 31). Why do you think the answer is so simple? What makes it hard to take at face value?
That same night the jailer "washed their wounds" and "set a meal before them" (vv. 33-34). What changed in him, and how might faith change the way we treat people we once saw as the other side?
If you are honest, where do you wonder whether God is guiding you at all, or whether he is quiet? What would help you keep going while you wait?
16.life: Pick one person who is on the edge of your life, such as a neighbor, a coworker or someone who is new. Invite them to a meal or a coffee this week, the way Lydia and the jailer opened their homes.
16.prayer: Thank God that he can work through closed doors and dark nights. Ask him to open your heart and your home, and to give steady trust to anyone in the group who feels stuck or unsure of the way ahead.
16.tip: Question 8 and the Spirit blocking Paul's plans can lead people to feel pressure to hear God clearly, or to feel left out if they never have. Say plainly that Paul's guidance here was unusual, and that Christians understand guidance in different ways. Keep the focus on trusting God while you move forward, and let quieter people say honestly where they feel unsure.

17.open: When you hear a new idea, are you the type to accept it quickly, check it out first, or push back? Why?
questions: In Thessalonica Paul spent three Sabbaths "explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead" (v. 3). Why might it have been surprising to hear that the Messiah would suffer?
The crowd called Paul and Silas men "who have turned the world upside down" (v. 6). What would it look like for someone today to be known that way for good reasons?
The Bereans "examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true" (v. 11). What helps you test what you hear, and what makes that hard?
Paul was "deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols" (v. 16). What do you notice around you that people look to for meaning or security? How do you tend to respond to it?

Paul began with the Athenians' own altar and even quoted their poets (vv. 23, 28). What do you take from the way he started where they were? Some Christians see this as a model for finding truth in other cultures, and others read it mainly as a call to turn away from them. How do you see it?

Paul says God "is not far from each one of us" and that people might "reach out for Him and find Him" (v. 27). Where have you felt close to God, or far from him? Feel free to be honest if the answer is far or unsure.
When Paul spoke of the resurrection, some of the Athenians mocked him, while others said they wanted to hear more about it (v. 32). Which reaction is closest to where you are right now, and why?
Some people believed and some walked away, and Paul seems to have accepted both. What does that say about how we should share our faith and handle the results?
17.life: Pick one person in your life who sees things differently. This week, ask them a real question about what they believe and listen without trying to answer or fix. Then pray for them by name.
17.prayer: Thank God that he is "not far from each one of us" (v. 27). Ask for honest curiosity like the Bereans had, and for gentleness and courage when you talk with people who see things differently.
17.tip: The Athens speech can turn into an argument about how Christians should relate to other religions and cultures. Say once that Christians read this differently, then bring the group back to what Paul actually does: he listens, starts from where people are, and still names Jesus and the resurrection. Leave room for the quiet person who is still searching.

18.open: Who is someone who taught you a practical skill, and what do you remember about how they did it?
questions: Paul "stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was" (v. 3). What does it say to you that Paul earned his living with his hands while he taught about Jesus?
When Paul was opposed and insulted, he said, "From now on I will go to the Gentiles" (v. 6), and then taught in the house next door. When has a door closed for you, and what did you find next to it?
The Lord told Paul, "Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent" (v. 9). Why might a strong, experienced person like Paul still need to hear that? Where do you need to hear it?
God said, "I have many people in this city" (v. 10). How does it change your view of your own neighborhood or workplace to think God already has people there?

Gallio called the complaint "a dispute about words and names and your own law" and refused to judge it (vv. 14-15). Why might some people see Christian faith as just an argument over words? How would you answer them?

Apollos was "eloquent" and "fervent in spirit," yet Priscilla and Aquila "took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately" (vv. 24-26). What do you notice about how they corrected him? What makes correction easier or harder to receive?

Paul said he would return "if God is willing" (v. 21). How do you hold your plans when you are unsure what God wants? If you are doubting or just unsure right now, what would an honest prayer about that sound like?
18.life: Think of someone who has helped you grow in faith, whether by teaching you or by quietly working alongside you. Write or call them this week to say thank you. If a friend could use a gentle word of help, pray first, then offer it privately and kindly.
18.prayer: Thank God that he is with us and already has people in the places we live and work. Ask for courage where we are afraid, and for humble hearts that can both teach and be taught.
18.tip: Verses 6 and 17 can raise questions about hostility toward Jewish people, so remind the group that Paul himself was Jewish and that the conflict here is a family argument, not a verdict on a whole people. Also, the vow in verse 18 and what Apollos was missing in verse 25 are unclear, and scholars are unsure. Say that briefly and move on to the bigger themes.

19.open: What is something you own or use that you would find really hard to give up, even if you knew you should?
questions: The twelve men in verses 1 to 7 had only known John's baptism. Paul told them John "told the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus" (v. 4). What do you think it was like to learn there was more to the story than they had known?

Verse 10 says that over two years "everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord." Paul taught daily in a lecture hall. What does that tell you about how the message spread, and what might that look like for us?

The sons of Sceva tried to use Jesus' name like a magic word, and the evil spirit answered, "Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?" (v. 15). What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and knowing him?
In verse 18 "many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds." Why might it be freeing, and also scary, to be honest about the past with other believers?

Those who had practiced magic arts burned their books in front of everyone, worth "fifty thousand drachmas" (v. 19). What might a costly step like that look like today, in work, money, habits or entertainment?

Demetrius said the business was "our source of prosperity" (v. 25), and the crowd shouted for two hours. How much do you think money and livelihood shape which ideas people are willing to hear? Where might that be true of us?
Verse 32 says that "most of them did not even know why they were there." When have you seen a crowd, online or in person, get loud and angry without knowing why? What helps us slow down?

If you are honest, where does your faith feel thin or uncertain right now? Verse 20 says "the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail." What would you want to say to God about that?
19.life: Pick one thing this week that quietly competes with God for your trust, such as a habit, a worry, or a source of security. Name it to God, and tell one trusted person about it.
19.prayer: Thank God that his word spreads and prevails even when people push back. Ask for honesty about what you have held onto, and for courage to let go of it.
19.tip: Verses 1 to 7 are the likely hard spot. Christians differ on whether receiving the Spirit can be a separate experience after first believing, as many Pentecostal churches hold, or whether this describes a one-time situation for people who had only known John's message. Say that in one line, then return to the chapter's bigger story.

20.open: Think of a goodbye you remember, at a station, a school gate or a front door. What made it stick with you?
questions: At Troas Paul kept talking "until midnight" and a young man fell from a window (vv. 7, 9). Have you ever struggled to stay awake or stay engaged in church or a study? What helps you, and what does the story suggest about how God treats us in those moments?

Verses 10 to 12 say Eutychus was "picked up dead," and the people were "greatly relieved" when he was taken home alive. Some readers think he truly died and others think he only seemed dead. What stands out to you about how the people responded?
Paul says he served "with great humility and with tears" (v. 19). What does it look like to serve people in a way that is humble and also honest about how much you care?

Paul says he "did not shrink back from declaring anything that was helpful" (v. 20). What is the difference between telling people hard truths and just being harsh? Who has done the first well for you?
In verse 24 Paul says he wants to "finish my course and complete the ministry I have received." What would it mean for you to finish well in the place God has put you right now?

Paul tells the elders, "Be shepherds of the church of God" and warns of "savage wolves" (vv. 28, 29). What are some ways a church or small group can stay healthy and protect each other, without becoming suspicious or controlling?
Paul quotes Jesus: "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (v. 35). When have you found that to be true, and when has it felt hard to believe?

Paul is heading toward chains and he does not know what will happen (vv. 22, 23). If you are in a season of uncertainty, or find it hard to trust God with what lies ahead, what would you honestly say to him about it?
20.life: Pick one person in your church, family or friendships and give them something this week, such as time, a meal, help with a task, or a note of encouragement. Do it quietly, and notice how it feels.
20.prayer: Thank God for the people who have cared for you like shepherds. Ask him to help you hold onto "the word of His grace" (v. 32), and to give courage to anyone in the group facing an uncertain road.
20.tip: The wolves in verses 29 and 30 can lead a group into naming names or arguing about who is teaching wrongly. Keep the focus on Paul's call to stay alert, to care for one another, and to rest on God's grace, and bring the conversation back to your own group's habits if it drifts.

21.open: Tell about a time you ignored good advice from someone who cared about you. How did it turn out?
questions: The believers in Tyre "kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem" (v. 4). Then the whole community, children included, knelt on the beach to pray with him (v. 5). What does that scene tell you about how they felt about Paul?
Agabus does not just speak. He ties up his own hands and feet with Paul's belt (v. 11). Why might God use a picture like that, and what does it add to words alone?

Paul says, "Why are you weeping and breaking my heart?" and then, "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus" (v. 13). What do you hear in his answer: courage, stubbornness, or something else? Why?

Many readers think the Spirit showed the believers the danger, and that the plea to stay away came from their own love. Christians disagree on whether Paul was right to go anyway. How do you tell the difference between a warning and a calling?
When Paul would not be persuaded, his friends said, "The Lord's will be done" (v. 14). When have you had to let someone you love make a risky choice? What was that like?

The elders ask Paul to join four men in a vow and pay their costs so people will know "there is no truth to these rumors about you" (v. 24). Some Christians see this as a wise gesture of peace, others as an uneasy compromise. What do you think it costs, and what does it gain, to go out of your way to calm a false rumor?

The charge in the temple was a guess, because the men had seen Trophimus "with him in the city, and they assumed" Paul had brought him in (v. 29). Where have you seen assumptions grow into something much bigger? How can we guard against that?

Paul has just been beaten and chained, yet he asks the commander, "May I say something to you?" and then asks to speak to the crowd (vv. 37, 39). If you are honest, where do you find it hard to trust God when things go badly, and what would help?
21.life: Think of one person whose advice you tend to brush off and one whose advice you always follow. This week, ask a trusted friend for honest counsel about a decision you are facing, and listen to the whole answer before you reply.
21.prayer: Ask God for wisdom to tell a warning from a calling, and for the humility to listen to people who love us. Pray for anyone in the group facing a hard choice or a false accusation.
21.tip: The question about whether Paul should have gone can turn into a debate with winners and losers. Say plainly that Christians read this differently, and bring the group back to what the chapter shows: Paul's friends loved him, Paul was sure of his course, and everyone ended up leaving it in God's hands.

22.open: Think of someone who once changed your mind about something big. What did they say or do that got through to you?
questions: Paul begins by saying, "I was just as zealous for God as any of you are today" (v. 3). Why might he start with what he shares with the crowd instead of where he disagrees with them?
Paul was sure he was serving God while he was hurting Jesus' followers. Have you ever been very sure about something and later found you were wrong? What did that teach you?
When the light flashed, Paul's first words to Jesus were a question: "Who are You, Lord?" (v. 8). What honest question would you ask God right now, even if you are not sure he will answer?
Paul's companions "saw the light, but they could not understand the voice" (v. 9). Why do you think people can be near the same moment and take away very different things about God?
Ananias greeted a man who had come to arrest believers with the words "Brother Saul" (v. 13). Who has welcomed you before you felt you deserved it, and who might need that kind of welcome from you?
Ananias asks, "what are you waiting for?" (v. 16). Is there a step of faith you have been putting off? What is holding you back?

In the temple, Paul pushes back on the Lord, arguing that his past should make people listen (vv. 19, 20). What does it tell you that he could speak so frankly in prayer, and that the answer was still "Go!" (v. 21)?
The crowd listened until Paul mentioned the Gentiles, then shouted, "Rid the earth of him!" (v. 22). What kinds of truth are hardest for us to hear, and why?
22.life: Write down your own story in a few plain sentences: what life was like before, how God has been meeting you, and what is different now. If you are still unsure about parts of it, write that honestly too. Share it with one person this week.
22.prayer: Thank God that he finds and changes people who are going the wrong way. Ask him to make you an honest witness to "what you have seen and heard" (v. 15), and to give you gentleness with those who disagree.
22.tip: Some people will feel their story is too small or too quiet next to Paul's dramatic one. Remind the group that Paul's story is one example and that God works in many ways. A slow, ordinary, or still unfolding story counts just as much.

23.open: Tell about a time something went wrong and help came from a place you did not expect.
questions: Paul opens with, "I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day" (v. 1). What does it take to have a clear conscience, and how do you know when yours can be trusted?

Paul is struck for speaking, and he answers sharply: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!" (v. 3). What do you notice about how he reacts? How do you tend to respond when you are treated unfairly?

Then Paul says he did not know the man was the high priest (v. 5). Some readers see an honest apology, and some see irony. Christians also differ on whether Paul's sharp words and his move to divide the council were courage or a slip. What do you make of this scene?
In verse 6 Paul says he is on trial over "my hope in the resurrection of the dead." Why would that hope matter so much to him, and what difference does it make for you?
Verse 11 says, "Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome." Why might Paul have needed to hear this after such a rough day?

More than forty men swear an oath to kill Paul (vv. 12-13), and the rescue comes through his sister's son (v. 16). What does it say about how God works that help can come through a young person nobody would expect?
The Roman commander protects Paul, though his letter makes himself look better than he was (vv. 27-29). What do you make of God working through people with mixed motives?
Paul is safe, yet he is still a prisoner under guard (v. 35). If you are in a season where God seems near but things are not fixed, what would you honestly say about that?
23.life: Think of one person who has quietly helped you, the way Paul's nephew helped him. This week, thank them in a note, a call or a text. If you are in a hard season, tell one trusted person about it.
23.prayer: Thank God that he stands near his people in the night, as he did with Paul. Ask for courage for anyone in the group facing something hard, and for honesty about what each person is carrying.
23.tip: Verses 3 to 5 can pull the group into a debate over whether Paul was right to speak that way. Name once that Christians read it differently, then steer back to verse 11 and the fact that God keeps his promise even when things look chaotic.

24.open: Think of a time you put off something you knew you needed to deal with, like a phone call, a doctor visit or a hard conversation. What finally got you to do it?
questions: Tertullus opens with praise for Felix, saying "we acknowledge this with all gratitude" (v. 3). Why do people flatter those in power, and when have you seen flattery used to get something?

Paul skips the flattery and sticks to the facts: he went to Jerusalem "to worship" and nobody found him "riling up a crowd" (vv. 11, 12). What does it tell you about Paul that he answers calmly and plainly?
Paul says he follows the Way, yet he also says he believes all that is written in the Law and the Prophets (v. 14). Why might it matter to him that his faith is rooted in what came before?
Paul says, "I strive always to maintain a clear conscience before God and man" (v. 16). What does a clear conscience look like in everyday life, and what makes it hard to keep?
Paul had been falsely accused, yet he spent two years under guard. How would you honestly feel in his place, and what would you want to say to God?

Felix "became frightened" when Paul spoke about "righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment" (v. 25). Why do you think those words hit him so hard, and how do you tend to react when something challenges you?

Felix said, "When I find the time, I will call for you" (v. 25), yet he kept talking with Paul, partly hoping for a bribe (v. 26). What are some ways we keep God at arm's length while staying near religious things?
If you are unsure what you believe about Jesus, or tired of waiting on God, what is one honest question or feeling you could share with the group tonight?
24.life: Pick one thing you have been putting off that your conscience keeps nudging you about, such as an apology, a decision or a prayer. Do one small step toward it this week, and ask God for help.
24.prayer: Ask God for a clear conscience and for the courage to answer his voice today instead of waiting for a better time. Pray for anyone in the group who is waiting on something hard.
24.tip: Felix is an easy character to judge, so the group may spend the whole time criticizing him. Gently turn it toward ourselves by asking where we tend to delay, and make space for anyone who is still unsure about faith to speak without pressure.

25.open: Have you ever had to explain something confusing to someone in charge, like a boss, a teacher or an official? How did it go?
questions: The leaders asked Festus for a favor because they were "preparing an ambush to kill him along the way" (v. 3). What does this tell you about how long and how deeply some people held their anger toward Paul?
Festus answered that Paul was being held in Caesarea and that the accusers could "accuse him there" (vv. 4-5). Why might a fair process matter so much when people are angry?
The accusers brought "many serious charges that they could not prove" (v. 7). When have you seen loud accusations get taken more seriously than the evidence behind them?
Paul says, "If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die" (v. 11). What do you notice about the way he stands up for himself here?

Paul used his right as a Roman citizen when he said, "I appeal to Caesar!" (v. 11). Do you think using the tools available to us, like laws or rights, fits with trusting God? How do the two go together for you?

Festus told Agrippa the dispute was about "a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive" (v. 19). If you had to describe your own belief about Jesus that plainly, how would you say it?

Festus admitted he "was at a loss" about these matters (v. 20) and was not sure what to do with Paul's claim. Where do you honestly feel at a loss about Jesus or faith right now? There are no wrong answers here.
Festus wanted to "do the Jews a favor" (v. 9), and it seems that pleasing people shaped his choices. Where do you feel pressure to keep people happy, and how does it affect what you do?
25.life: Think of someone whose deepest belief seems strange to you. This week, ask them one sincere question about it and listen to the whole answer without arguing.
25.prayer: Thank God that he is with his people even when they are falsely accused or stuck waiting. Ask for the courage to speak honestly and the patience to listen well.
25.tip: Paul's appeal to Caesar can lead to a debate about whether Christians should use legal rights or just trust God. Keep it gentle: note that Paul did both, telling the truth plainly and using his rights, and let people share how they see it without needing one answer.

26.open: Have you ever changed your mind about something you used to feel strongly about? What caused the change?
questions: Paul begins by saying he is "fortunate" to speak to Agrippa because the king knows Jewish customs and controversies (vv. 2-3). Why might it matter to Paul to be heard by someone who understands the real issue?
Paul says he lived as a Pharisee, "adhering to the strictest sect of our religion" (v. 5). Why do you think he starts with his background before he talks about Jesus?

Paul admits, "In my raging fury against them, I even went to foreign cities to persecute them" (v. 11). What is it like to hear someone tell the worst part of their own story so plainly? Why might he include it?

On the road Jesus says, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?" and then, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting" (vv. 14-15). What stands out to you about how Jesus speaks to a man who is working against him?

Jesus sends Paul "to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light" (v. 18). What do you think it means to have your eyes opened? When has that happened for you, or when would you like it to?
Paul says, "I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision" (v. 19). What does obeying look like for an ordinary person today, when there is no bright light or voice from heaven?

Festus shouts, "You are insane, Paul!" and Agrippa asks, "Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?" (vv. 24, 28). Scholars read Agrippa's tone in different ways. How do you respond when someone's faith seems too much, or when you feel unsure about your own?

Paul answers, "I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains" (v. 29). What does this show about how he feels toward the people judging him?
26.life: Write out your own story in a few sentences: what life was like before you trusted Jesus, how things changed, and what is true now. If you are still unsure, write where you are honestly. Share it with one person this week, or simply with God.
26.prayer: Thank God that he reaches people who are working against him, as he reached Paul. Ask him to open the eyes of those in your life who are far from him, and to give each of you honesty and gentleness in how you tell your own story.
26.tip: Paul's conversion is dramatic, and some people in the group may feel their own story is too quiet or too uncertain to count. Say plainly that Paul's story is one example, not a template, and that many people come to faith slowly, with doubts still in tow. Give those people room to speak first.

27.open: Tell about a time a trip or plan went badly off course. What did you do?
questions: Paul warned that the voyage would end in "disaster and great loss" (v. 10), but the centurion went with the pilot and the owner of the ship instead (v. 11). Why do you think people listen to the experts or the majority and not to the quiet voice? When have you done the same?

The crew threw cargo and then the ship's tackle overboard, and in the end "we abandoned all hope of being saved" (vv. 18-20). What does it look like when people finally let go of things they thought they needed?
An angel told Paul, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar" (v. 24). Paul was a prisoner in a storm, and yet he was the one giving courage. What do you think made that possible?

Paul says, "I believe God that it will happen just as He told me" (v. 25). What is one thing you find hard to believe God about right now? You can answer honestly, even if the answer is that you are not sure.
Paul says the sailors must stay on board or "you cannot be saved" (v. 31), even though God had promised everyone's life. How do you hold together God's promise and our own responsibility to act?

In verse 35 Paul "took bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all," and then they were "all encouraged." What does that simple act tell us about how faith can show up in an ordinary, frightening moment?

The centurion stopped the soldiers from killing the prisoners because he wanted "to spare Paul's life" (v. 43), and so everyone was saved. What does it say about God that other people were helped because Paul was there?
The ship was lost, but every life was saved (v. 44). When have you come through something with the loss of something big, yet found you were still held?
27.life: This week, think of one person who is in a storm of their own, such as illness, work trouble or a family strain. Do one steady, practical thing for them, like sharing a meal, sending a message or sitting with them.
27.prayer: Thank God that he is present in the storms we did not choose and the ones we helped cause. Ask for steady hearts and for honest trust, even when it is small.
27.tip: Questions 4 and 8 may stir up real pain, since some people have prayed for rescue and not received it. Do not rush to tidy it up. Let the quiet ones answer in a sentence, and remind the group that Paul's promise here was for this situation and not a guarantee that every storm ends the same way.

28.open: Tell about a time someone's kindness caught you off guard, maybe when you were tired, lost or having a bad day.
questions: The shipwrecked travelers were cold and soaked, and the islanders "showed us extraordinary kindness" (v. 2). When has someone's kindness reached you at a low point, and what did it do for you?

The islanders first said, "Surely this man is a murderer," then changed their minds and said "he was a god" (vv. 4, 6). Both guesses came from one snakebite. When have you seen someone judged quickly by a single event, and what did the judgment miss?

Paul healed Publius's father "after praying and placing his hands on him" (v. 8). What do you notice about the prayer coming first? If you have prayed for healing and not seen it, how has that sat with you?
Believers walked a long way out from Rome to meet Paul, and "he was encouraged and gave thanks to God" (v. 15). Who has shown up for you like that? Who could you go out of your way to meet this week?

Paul is under guard and says he is "bound with this chain" (v. 20), yet he spends his days talking about hope. Where do you feel stuck or limited right now, and what might faithfulness look like there?

After a full day of Paul's teaching, "Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe" (v. 24). Why do people hear the same message so differently? Where would you honestly place yourself today: convinced, unsure or somewhere in between?

Paul says God's salvation "has been sent to the Gentiles" (v. 28), yet he keeps "welcoming all who came to visit him" (v. 30). Christians read these verses differently, some as a final turning away from the Jewish people and others as one more step in an ongoing pattern. What do you notice in verses 28 to 31 as you read them together?
The book ends with Paul teaching "boldly and freely" while still in custody (v. 31). What would speaking or living boldly and freely look like in your ordinary week?
28.life: Think of one person who is far from home, new to your area, or going through a hard stretch. Reach out this week with something practical, like a meal, a ride or a visit, the way the islanders and the Roman believers did for Paul.
28.prayer: Thank God for the people who have welcomed and encouraged you. Ask for open hands and open doors, and for boldness to share the hope of Jesus with kindness.
28.tip: Verses 26 to 28 can be misheard as a harsh word against the Jewish people. Remind the group that Paul is Jewish, that Isaiah was a Jewish prophet grieving over his own people, and that Paul keeps welcoming everyone in verse 30. Keep the focus on how people respond to the message, not on any group.
